items.title_orig: Jeff Ament Looks Back at Pearl Jam’s Early Days — and Explains How They Picked Their New Drummer
items.article_text:
Pearl Jam bassist Jeff Ament is also a photographer, and you already know his work: He shot the sheep close-up on the cover of 1993’s Vs., as well as the covers of 1998’s Yield, 2002’s Riot Act, and the 2003 rarities collection Lost Dogs. He’s also been turning his camera on his bandmates since the early Nineties. His excellent new book, Since Forever — created with his brother, designer Barry Ament — collects more than 250 of those black-and-white photos, along with his written reflections.

The book came out Sept. 25, the same night Pearl Jam played their first show since Matt Cameron left, a surprise appearance at the Ohana Festival  — with longtime Paul McCartney drummer Abe Laboriel Jr. behind the kit. Vedder told the crowd Laboriel was helping out for the night, and the band hasn’t said whether he’s joined for good. Pearl Jam headline the festival tonight.

In the new episode of Rolling Stone Music Now, Ament breaks down the stories behind the photos in Since Forever, and goes deep on Pearl Jam’s early days, touring with Neil Young, the band’s next chapter, and much more. To hear the whole episode, listen on Apple Podcasts or Spotify, or just press play above. Here are some highlights from the discussion:

Ament sold his camera to move to Seattle in 1983, and only got a new one when the Singles production told him to charge it to the movie. “Those first two, three years that I lived in Seattle, there’s literally, like, five pictures,” Ament says. “That was the sacrifice I had to make. I had to sell my camera to move to Seattle. That was the high-dollar item. I think I got 100 bucks for it or something, which was a lot of money in 1983.” That changed when Cameron Crowe brought him into the art department for Singles. “They needed pictures of something, and I said, ‘I don’t have a camera,’ and they were like, ‘Go get a camera.’ And I’m like, ‘What do you mean?’ And they’re like, ‘Dude, just go get a camera and charge it to the movie.’ And I was like, ‘I can do that?'”

Ament’s DIY streak kicked in when he learned that a photographer hired by the label might charge $8,000 for an hour, and that Pearl Jam was footing at least half the bill. “The funny thing is, a lot of that early stuff, I wasn’t trying to document,” Ament says. “I was trying to come up with content for albums we were making, or at some point pretty early on, we were putting out newsletters, and we needed content for those newsletters. And even with album covers, it became apparent early on, like, you know, the label would hire a photographer, and then you’d find out that we were paying for it or we were paying for half of it, and a photographer charged like $8,000 or something for an hour. And there was like that frugal DIY part of me that was like, ‘That’s ridiculous, man. Like, that’s four times more than my camera equipment’s worth. Like, I can do this shit.'” Ament was surprised to see he had shot photos of a shirtless Eddie Vedder in the vocal booth during the recording sessions for Ten. “Looking at the contact sheets, I didn’t know what those photos were,” Ament says. “You’re just going like, ‘Man, that’s weird. There’s three photos in a row of, like, just the dark side of the studio.’ And then when we digitize them and you put them on the screen, all of a sudden it’s like, oh, he’s singing in the booth there.” He didn’t clear the shots with the band. “Hopefully he’s cool with me,” he says. “I didn’t run any of this [by them].” As for the missing shirt: “‘Cause it was fucking hot, man. Those isolation rooms, they didn’t have any air in them, so I’m surprised he didn’t have his Speedo on. Not that he has a Speedo, but…”

The sheep on the cover of Vs. was following Ament along a fence on a Montana farm. He had no idea he was shooting an album cover. “I could tell that this one sheep was following me along the fence, so I just started taking pictures of it, and it just kept trying to get through the fence,” Ament says. “It was only when I got the contact sheet back, I was like, ‘Wow, that’d be a great cover,’ ’cause we’d already written ‘Animal,’ and there was a little bit of feeling of us against the world at that time, and us against the record company, us against, you know, whatever the machine. And so it sort of felt … so much more natural than the first album cover that was, you know, very literal. … It was cool to put the whole contact sheet, or most of the contact sheet, in there just to show people that I wasted a whole roll of film on that.” For the record, Ament thinks it’s a sheep, not an Angora goat, as some accounts have it.

When Pearl Jam backed Neil Young on the 1995 Mirror Ball tour, Young would spring songs on them 20 minutes before showtime. “Almost every show he’d come back like 20 minutes before the show and he’d be like, ‘Hey, think we’re gonna do “Mr. Soul” tonight,'” Ament says. “And we’d be scrambling around, like, pulling out a cassette of Decade. … Luckily Brendan [O’Brien] had played a lot of those songs in bands when he was a kid, so he sort of knew what was going on. But we would literally be back there with our instruments, learning the song, and then we’d go out in Berlin and play the song for the first time ever. Just hanging on by the seat of our pants.” Young took the same approach onstage: “He would just decide, like, ‘We’re doing a 15-minute version of this song tonight,’ and sort of, like, hit a couple of his pedals and his amps would get really loud, and you just have to come along.”

Ament and Matt Cameron used to joke that they had about three years left in Pearl Jam. Ament was kidding. Cameron, it turned out, wasn’t. “He and I even joked sometimes, like we would say, like, ‘So what we got, like three more years left …?’ And he’d be like, ‘Yeah, yeah. That sounds about right. Three more years.’ Like, ‘So we’ll both be 60. Yeah, that’ll be perfect,'” Ament says. “And I think it would maybe make the other guys a little bit nervous. But I was joking, and then it turns out that he wasn’t. … And I get it, man. You get to be 60 and we’re lucky to be here at 60 still. But you also have, like, maybe some unrealized dreams and other things you wanna do, and maybe the unrealized dream is like you just wanna sit at home with your wife. Could be just as simple as that.” Still, Ament isn’t ready to stop. “Every once in a while we have a show where I’m like, ‘Ah, fuck, man. I’ll put that up against any 25-year-old band,'” he says. “I just fucking love hanging out with these guys so much.”

Pearl Jam’s new drummer was everyone’s first choice.  “It was the first name that came up. … In our minds, let’s start at the top,” Ament says. “And all of us have, like, really good friends who are drummers. … The hardest part was, like, telling … my friends who are, like, killer drummers that we had a guy.” Speaking before the reveal, Ament wasn’t ready to call it permanent: “I hope this is our guy, but I don’t know if it is. We haven’t played a show yet, so it’s pretty hard to be fully committed.” When it’s suggested the new drummer might turn out to be a robot, Ament plays along, referring to the band’s endless takes of “Even Flow”: “We finally got the ‘Even Flow’ thing figured out. It really sits back on the choruses. We programmed it into this drum machine. It’s amazing. You’re gonna love it.”

Ament wants Pearl Jam to make a new album and tour next year. “I would love that,” he says of the possibility. “We’re sort of due. … It’s like we have some new energy, and like, we just have an opportunity to use that energy to the fullest and turn it into something different and something great.” The band has only just started writing new music. “I think everybody’s writing, but we haven’t really written a whole bunch of stuff together, but a couple of things that we have done are really good. So I think we understand the potential. … The time apart, you sort of sit with, like, ‘Oh, shit, I can’t wait to do this.’ I’m chomping at the bit. … But it’s gonna take a littl…

items.title_orig: Tyler Childers Brings the Wild, Eddie Vedder Surprise Performs at Ohana Festival
items.article_text:
By sunset on the second day of Eddie Vedder‘s annual Ohana Festival in Dana Point, California, the sky was a fury of tangerine ribbons and set the stage for the evening’s top acts, who brought bold performances of unity to the heart of Orange County.

Tyler Childers, who headlined Saturday, brought his message of loving thy neighbor — echoing an earlier speech by Alabama Shakes frontwoman Brittany Howard, who wore an “ICE OUT” pin during the band’s set — to his signature ferocious performance. And at twilight, New Orleans bandleader and composer Jon Batiste delivered a contagious tour-de-force of joy and struggle, careening from ragtime classics to contemporary numbers.

A large part of Saturday’s top slots were dedicated to country acts, and several musicians weaved in songs of everyday Americans and calls of solidarity. Earlier in the day, during Stephen Wilson Jr.’s standout afternoon show, the rising Nashville star (and former microbiologist) took a playful jab at AI before launching into his working class salute, “Gary.”

“This is for all our fixers out there that show up and get our lives back on track. Cause I do not believe AI will show up at your dorm when life hits the fan,” Wilson told the crowd. “But I do believe AI will and if his name is Gary, you’re probably in pretty good shape.” Behind Wilson was a tiny robot held captive in a birdcage.

Mid-way though his set, Vedder surprised the crowd and joined Wilson on stage for an excellent rendition of “Hunger Strike,” the Temple of the Dog track originally sung by Vedder and Chris Cornell. It was one of several cameos by Vedder this weekend, who joined Bad Religion on Friday to sing “American Jesus.” (Vedder originally provided backing vocals on the 1993 Recipe for Hate track.)

Batiste and his band took to the stage right before sunset and performed a nonstop medley that put his spin on New Orleans jazz, gospel, soul, and funk. The hour-long celebration saw Batiste dance across the stage as he moved from the piano, saxophone, and melodica, and included a majestic performance of “Freedom” from his Grammy-winning album We Are that was amplified by the indomitable Desiree “Desz” Washington. At one point, Batiste led the crowd as thousands sang Leonard Cohen’s “Hallelujah,” then amped it up with a rollicking rendition of “When the Saints Go Marching In.”

After the sun dipped behind the ocean, Alabama Shakes, who dropped their first album in 11 years, I Must Be Dreaming, last month, delivered a dazzling performance that stretched back to their 2012 debut album, Boys & Girls, alongside Sound & Color tracks “Guess Who” and “Dunes.” Their set also brought offerings from their latest LP, including their standout, “American Dream.”

Howard paused the show to address the audience in the heart of Orange County’s conservative enclave. “I was thinking about people who risk their life, living to protect each other, protect their communities, protect their neighbors, protect our rights, and when I see that, it gives me hope for our future,” said Howard. “At the end of it all, it’s really just us taking care of each other.” Her message was met with cheers from the crowd.

While not originally scheduled, Florence Road performed during the break before Childers’ headlining set. The Irish rock band was set to play on Friday afternoon but hit a snag when their gear was stolen from their van that day. Luckily, fest organizers were able to squeeze them into an evening slot. Lead singer Lily Aron thanked Vedder and his crew for putting the band “on this gorgeous stage at this gorgeous time.”

As Childers closed out the night, the “Long Violent History” singer drew in the crowd with his stage set up like a living room with lamps, a console TV, and wood chair strewn around his band. Childers opened with lead Snipe Hunter track, the searing “Eatin’ Big Time.” After following up with the “randy” title track “Rustin’ in the Rain” from his 2015 album, Childers sang the more “appropriately considered” love song and fan-favorite “All Your’n.”

Childers proceeded to tear through an exhilarating lineup that included the likes of the yearning “Oneida,” toothy “Dirty Ought Trill,” and the ornery, tall-tale telling “Whitehouse Road.” At one point in the night, he had the crowd literally barking and howling in ode to his rabies-wishing “Bitin’ List.” He ended the end with the gut-wrenching “Lady May,” the one song he hopes to remeber if he’s “hit in the head tomorrow and I couldn’t remember anything that I ever wrote or played.”

Before bidding adieu to the crowd, Childers left the audience with a neighborly invite to get to know someone in the crowd. “One of the most important things that you’ve had the opportunity to partake in this evening, other than listening to music, one of the most important things above all the clinking jangling of the keys and the beating of the strings and the banging of the drums, the one biggest, most important thing that you’ve had the opportunity to do is a little bit of fellowship,” he said in one breathless delivery.
